rows.original_exact: An early experiment illustrated this problem. For a course project in ME 610: Neuromechanical Modeling, Morrow and I coupled the bipedal mechanics of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} with the two-level central pattern generator (CPG) of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} in AnimatLab \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. The model included bilateral thigh, shank, foot, and toe segments, sagittal-plane joints, and antagonist Hill-type muscles. I added a passive toe joint. A shared rhythm generator (RG) supplied pattern-formation (PF) and motor-neuron (MN) pathways on both sides. We adjusted currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters manually and presented the suspended result at the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. The legs cycled when suspended, but the model lost support when released toward the ground (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}). The continued neural rhythm did not establish an effective load-bearing controller.

rows.original_exact: This chapter addresses the fourth dissertation objective by developing tools for constructing and testing coupled neural and mechanical models. The methods connect OpenSim- and CAD-derived mechanics, graphical neural construction, actuator and sensory interfaces, staged calibration, and automated experiments. The results proceed from mechanical and circuit checks to coupled responses, controlled interventions, and computational performance. OpenSim, MyoConverter, MuJoCo, SNS-Toolbox, Simulink, and Simscape provide the existing software foundations \citep{delp_opensim_2007,caggiano_myosuite_2022,todorov_mujoco_2012,nourse_sns_2023}. My contributions are the model preparation and repairs, editable blocks, actuator integrations, and experiment procedures that connect those foundations. Appendix~\ref{app:simulation_verification} gives supporting configurations, source scripts, and secondary comparisons.
rows.revised_exact: I built on OpenSim, MyoConverter, MuJoCo, SNS-Toolbox, Simulink, and Simscape \citep{delp_opensim_2007,caggiano_myosuite_2022,todorov_mujoco_2012,nourse_sns_2023}. My contribution was to prepare mechanical models, implement editable neural and actuator blocks, connect neural outputs with actuator commands and mechanical measurements with sensory inputs, and write drivers that repeat interventions with a saved controller. The methods below describe how to assemble an experiment. The results start with a single joint, then examine how sensory return and mechanical assistance change bilateral coordination. Appendix~\ref{app:simulation_verification} gives the executable examples and scoring definitions.

rows.original_exact: The SNS-Simscape library implements neurons, chemical synapses, sensory encoders, activation dynamics, and muscle-force elements as editable Simulink blocks (Figure~\ref{fig:simulink_sns_implementation}). It retains the conductance-based formulations used by SNS-Toolbox \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Synapses supply conductance and conductance--reversal-potential products; the postsynaptic neuron combines these with its membrane state and other currents. Membrane voltage and normalized motor command remain distinct signals. This organization permits inspection of individual pathways and the calculations they perform.
rows.revised_exact: I implemented the SNS-Simscape library as editable Simulink blocks for neurons, synapses, sensory encoding, activation, and actuator force (Figure~\ref{fig:simulink_sns_implementation}). The graded equations follow SNS-Toolbox \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Each synapse sends a conductance and its product with reversal potential to the postsynaptic neuron. This makes the sign and strength of a connection available for inspection. From the \path{Code/Matlab/SNS_Simscape/gui} directory, running \verb|app = SNSGui()| opens my circuit editor. A user can place and connect graded neurons, save the circuit description, and generate a Simulink circuit through \path{sns_build_from_json.m}. Separate builders connect complete reflex circuits to the knee and arm dynamics.

rows.original_exact: The complete feedback loop connects MN output to activation or a pressure command, the actuator model to tensile force, and the mechanical state to sensory encoding. Length, lengthening velocity, and force provide inputs for Ia, II, and Ib pathways; foot contact supplies a distinct event or load signal. Their encoding ranges, signs, saturation, and update intervals must be stated. A synaptic conductance is not itself a sensory force, and a normalized neural output is not a pressure until the command mapping defines that conversion. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_signal_contracts} records these interface distinctions.
rows.revised_exact: In the reduced knee, extensor and flexor MN outputs pass through activation dynamics to antagonist tensile actuators. Their moments change the knee angle and angular velocity. The spindle-like transducers use joint motion to produce Ia currents, and the Ib transducers use actuator tension. Each Ia pathway excites its own MN and inhibits the antagonist. Each Ib pathway inhibits its own MN. The resulting six connections close the loop that the worked example tests. The Gait2392 and W2L experiments use different sensory encoders and input ports, identified in Appendix~\ref{sec:app_signal_contracts}.

rows.original_exact: For block-programmed control of MuJoCo mechanics, I integrated the SNS blocks with the MathWorks MuJoCo--Simulink bridge. Actuator commands enter the mechanical simulation, and joint and actuator measurements return through its sensor interface. Local compatibility and initialization fixes establish the appropriate model state before signal exchange. The bridge retains the selected mechanical timestep and supports different controller and mechanical update rates. Neural and mechanical updates in the reported Gait2392 controller experiments use a \qty{2}{\milli\second} interval; the bridge two-rate test uses a \qty{1}{\milli\second} command-source interval and a \qty{5}{\milli\second} mechanical/sensor interval. Each test retains its actual integration settings.
rows.revised_exact: For experiments with MuJoCo mechanics, I integrated the blocks with the MathWorks MuJoCo--Simulink bridge and adapted initialization and sensor readback. A Simulink controller sends an ordered actuator-command array to MuJoCo and reads the resulting joint and actuator measurements. I tested a command source updated every \qty{1}{\milli\second} with a mechanical and sensor update every \qty{5}{\milli\second}. The separate Gait2392 neural and mechanical experiments used \qty{2}{\milli\second} updates.

rows.original_exact: Neural calibration then selects parameters for these declared functions. I implemented the four operations presented by \citet{hunt_inrc_2019}: establish an intrinsic rhythm with a period approximately twice the target locomotor period; tune entrainment using expected afferent signals; fit feedforward motor recruitment; and refine the motor pattern with sensory feedback. Expected activation targets are inverse-mechanics estimates from reference motion, rather than measured electromyograms. Their agreement with MN output measures the stated calibration target, not biological validation of every neural pathway.
rows.revised_exact: I adapted the four calibration operations presented by \citet{hunt_inrc_2019}. I set the intrinsic period to approximately twice the target locomotor period, tuned entrainment under expected afferent input, fitted feedforward motor recruitment, and refined the pattern with sensory feedback. The recruitment targets came from inverse mechanics applied to reference motion. Agreement with those targets measures how well the network reproduces the estimated activation pattern.

rows.original_exact: Mechanical inspection exposed faults that would otherwise have been attributed to controller behavior. Repairs addressed selected joint-action signs, active force scales, coupled path-point limits, and intended ground contacts. At matched poses and OpenSim static-optimization activations, eight of twelve sampled muscles had force-prediction $R^2$ between 0.87 and 0.98 and mean forces within \qty{10}{\percent} of the reference (Table~\ref{tab:force-r2}). Rectus femoris and biceps femoris short head had negative $R^2$. Thus, the comparison identified useful agreement and important remaining muscle-specific differences. It assigned pose and activation frame by frame, without reproducing trajectory velocities or tendon dynamics, and consequently did not establish dynamic equivalence of the muscle formulations.
rows.revised_exact: At matched poses and OpenSim static-optimization activations, eight of twelve sampled muscles gave force-prediction $R^2$ values of 0.87--0.98 and mean forces within \qty{10}{\percent} of the reference (Table~\ref{tab:force-r2}). Rectus femoris and biceps femoris short head had negative $R^2$. For those muscles, the mean reference force predicted the sampled force better than the converted model did. This comparison prescribed a pose and activation for each frame. Movement velocity and tendon dynamics were outside its scope.

rows.original_exact: Bridge tests established that a block-programmed controller could deliver muscle commands and receive the corresponding measurements. Single-muscle activation, different control rates, and sensor readback were compared with Python MuJoCo integration. The five tested sensor arrays were bit-exact over 80 steps from \qty{0.005}{\second} to \qty{0.400}{\second}, excluding the initial sample. A separate exported network drove all 92 actuator channels during a \qty{5}{\second} run, and a closed-loop reflex experiment exercised both command and sensory return. These results verify the interface operations under their stated conditions.
rows.revised_exact: The bridge delivered the prescribed muscle commands from Simulink to MuJoCo. All five tested sensor arrays matched Python readback bit for bit over 80 steps from \qty{0.005}{\second} through \qty{0.400}{\second}. An exported neural circuit drove all 92 actuator channels for \qty{5}{\second}. A separate reflex test returned mechanical measurements to the controller. Its length encoder saturated after initialization, so the experiment demonstrates bidirectional signal exchange while leaving sensitivity to length untested (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_signal_contracts}).
rows.context: Matched poses, bridge, circuit and supported W2L rhythm-core tests

rows.original_exact: The contact-driven W2L comparison tested a representative 26-neuron Simulink rhythm core against the corresponding signals of the 95-neuron NumPy network. The core used corresponding neuron parameters and shared pathways under identical drive and prescribed heel inputs. Over the post-startup \qtyrange{2}{12}{\second} window, burst periods matched at \qty{1.000}{\second} and all ten expected bursts were reproduced. Best-lag correlation of the four shared RG voltage traces was at least 0.99996, allowing a \qty{2}{\milli\second} relative alignment lag (Figure~\ref{fig:w2l_crossengine}). Removing the phasic heel input caused both realizations to latch. This verifies the tested shared rhythm core and input dependence, rather than complete-network or unshifted sample agreement.
rows.revised_exact: A contact-driven W2L test compared a 26-neuron Simulink rhythm core with the corresponding four RG signals in the 95-neuron NumPy network. With identical drive and prescribed heel inputs, both produced all ten expected bursts with a \qty{1.000}{\second} period over \qtyrange{2}{12}{\second}. The four best-lag voltage correlations were at least 0.99996 with a \qty{2}{\milli\second} relative alignment (Figure~\ref{fig:w2l_crossengine}). Removing phasic heel input caused both circuits to latch. The comparison verifies the shared rhythm-generating pathways under this stimulus.

rows.original_exact: Reduced reflex models then tested the closed loop. The knee example contains homonymous Ia excitation, reciprocal Ia inhibition, and homonymous Ib inhibition for each antagonist, giving six feedback connections (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_reflex_current}). A \qty{2}{\nano\ampere}, \qty{30}{\milli\second} pulse at the extensor Ia sensory input produced \ang{1.09} of extension, peaking \qty{111}{\milli\second} after onset. The response met the specified recovery thresholds after \qty{6.355}{\second}. Broadened MN and Ia saturation ramps produced this graded transient; the earlier narrow ramps maintained oscillations. The actuators in this reduced knee test use the simplified linear BPA-force element. It is a numerical circuit-response test, not a physiologically calibrated tendon tap or validation of the complete Festo force surface.
rows.revised_exact: A researcher can reproduce the knee experiment with \path{run_transient.m} and the archived \texttt{KneeReflexDemo} model. The driver runs the settled knee twice and adds a \qty{2}{\nano\ampere}, \qty{30}{\milli\second} pulse to the extensor Ia current in one run. The pulse recruited the extensor MN. The flexor was already inactive, so the rise in extensor force accounted for the initial extension (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_reflex_current}). The stimulated knee extended \ang{1.09} relative to the control, peaked \qty{111}{\milli\second} after pulse onset, and met the angle and speed recovery criteria \qty{6.355}{\second} after onset. Broader MN and Ia synaptic operating ranges allowed the model to settle before the pulse. The original narrow ranges produced sustained oscillation. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_knee_transient} gives the MATLAB command and the fields to inspect in the saved summary.
rows.context: Knee pulse from t=30 s or cup ramp t=10 s, 0.625 kg

rows.original_exact: In the loaded-cup experiment, the arm sagged by \ang{2.00} with feedback enabled, compared with \ang{7.85} when disabled, at the \qty{10}{\second} endpoint of the loading ramp (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_beverage_current}). The applied mass reaches \qty{0.625}{\kilogram} at that endpoint; the comparison is not an equilibrium measurement. Biceps stretch excites its own MN and reciprocally inhibits the triceps MN; each Ib pathway inhibits its homonymous MN. This example uses the BPA20 force block and its stated command mapping. The matched loading comparison demonstrates a corrective effect of these pathways in the coupled model. It does not establish human reflex gains or measured pneumatic pressure dynamics. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_knee_transient} supplies the more detailed numerical checks for the knee response.
rows.revised_exact: The loaded-cup model uses the pressure-dependent BPA20 force block in the arm. Increasing the simulated cup mass to \qty{0.625}{\kilogram} over \qty{10}{\second} produced \ang{7.85} of sag with feedback disabled and \ang{2.00} with the graded feedback circuit enabled (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_beverage_current}). The matched spiking circuit gave \ang{1.78} at the same ramp endpoint (Appendix~\ref{sec:spiking_results}). As the arm descended, biceps stretch recruited the biceps and inhibited its antagonist. This reduced the sag while the load was still increasing.
rows.context: Knee pulse from t=30 s or cup ramp t=10 s, 0.625 kg

rows.original_exact: The revised graded BiW2Lvar+ controller completed both air stages with the same learned weights and shared PF-to-MN expression scale of 0.1. In the \qty{16}{\second} deafferented test, the principal-cycle audit detected four cycles on each side, a \qty{2.466}{\second} period, and 0.0337-cycle error from bilateral antiphase. The afferented test produced seven cycles per side, a \qty{1.300}{\second} period, and 0.0933-cycle phase error (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_biw2l_air}). The retained adapter defines stage 1 with sensory return and sustained flexor/extensor commands disabled, and stage 2 with live sensory return and both normalized commands set to 0.15 bilaterally. Complete applied-command histories and the original launch adapter were not recovered, so these definitions cannot establish sample-by-sample command identity in the original runs. The period change therefore cannot be interpreted as a controlled feedback-only effect. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_biw2l_air} gives the initialization and retained assessments.
rows.revised_exact: The revised graded BiW2Lvar+ controller completed both \qty{16}{\second} suspended trials with the same learned weights and PF-to-MN expression scale of 0.1. From \qty{5}{\second} to just before \qty{14}{\second}, the detector found four principal knee-flexion peaks per side in the first trial and seven in the second. The corresponding periods were \qty{2.466}{\second} and \qty{1.300}{\second}, with bilateral timing errors of 0.0337 and 0.0933 cycles from antiphase (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_biw2l_air}). The retained adapter specifies two changes between trials. It enables sensory return and raises the sustained normalized flexor and extensor commands from zero to 0.15 on both sides. The original launch adapter and complete command histories were unavailable, and the period difference cannot be assigned to feedback alone.

rows.original_exact:
Fixed-weight noise tests examined the same air-stage candidate under continuous disturbances to RG input current. Three independent seeds were tested at each stationary standard deviation, \qtylist{0.01;0.025}{\nano\ampere}, with a \qty{20}{\milli\second} correlation time. All six trials retained the specified duration, principal motion, frontal separation, and knee bounds. A fresh-process repeated seed reproduced the noise, neural states, and joint states exactly. This tests suspended coordination under the stated current noise; it does not establish ground-balance robustness or tolerance to arbitrary connection changes (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_current_noise}).

Layer-specific stimuli also depended on operating phase. A \qty{2}{\nano\ampere}, \qty{100}{\milli\second} pulse to the right hip-flexor PF channel at \qty{7.10}{\second} changed its voltage without crossing the outgoing rest-relative \qty{0}{\milli\volt} transmission threshold and produced essentially no MN response. With onset at \qty{7.65}{\second}, during an active phase, the same pulse changed PF voltage by up to \qty{1.14}{\milli\volt} and right iliacus MN voltage by \qty{0.16}{\milli\volt}. These maxima compare paired trajectories during the \qty{3.4}{\second} response window beginning at onset. A direct right iliacus MN pulse subsequently affected RG activity through the closed mechanical and sensory loop. These paired tests show why stimulation site, operating phase, and observation window must be identified before interpreting a response (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_biw2l_stimulus}).
rows.context: BiW2Lvar+ 16 s air runs, cadence at 5 ≤ t < 14 s; 5–16 s spring support; phase-locked stimuli

rows.original_exact: A historical fixed-controller W2L comparison tested the contribution of sensory return to bilateral ground-contact coordination. With conductances, drive, and support held fixed, disabling the saved sensory-feedback channels shifted median bilateral contact phase from 0.498 to 0.223 cycles. The accepted interval was 0.35--0.65 cycles, centered on antiphase. Joint cycling and forward displacement persisted: displacement over \qtyrange{4.5}{30}{\second} was \qty{2.239}{\meter} with feedback and \qty{1.996}{\meter} without it. The retained evaluator also specifies a common \qty{40}{\newton} forward pulse from \qty{8}{\second} to \qty{8.15}{\second} in both conditions; an unforced baseline was not established by this pair. The result identifies a contribution to contact coordination under those matched inputs, rather than a requirement for all rhythmic movement (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_ablation_pair}). Additional pathway controls are retained in Appendix~\ref{sec:app_w2l_perturbations}.

Median bilateral contact phase shifted from 0.498 to 0.223 cycles, outside the accepted 0.35--0.65 interval around antiphase. \FloatBarrier
Intermediate verification exposed a different limitation in the s3k and syn6 human-model controllers. Their offline MN-output fits could satisfy an activation-error criterion without reproducing the intended PF timing. In syn6, none of twelve channels passed the combined provisional timing checks. Actual PF activity required three components per side to explain \qty{99}{\percent} of centered variance, compared with six for the intended primitives, and one channel remained active throughout the cycle. The corresponding s3k activity required two components per side, while quantitative intended PF windows had not been declared. These are descriptions of the measured signals, not minimum neuron counts.
rows.context: Historical W2L intervention, 30 s protocol with 8–8.15 s common disturbance; syn6 timing checkpoints

rows.original_exact: A bounded syn6 gain-only repair improved its fitting loss but still passed none of the twelve channel checks. Subsequent RG-triggered relays and native SNS timing circuits addressed the failed function directly. The native circuit passed all 48 channel-cycle checks at the nominal cadence, and adaptive clocks extended that result to six controlled replay cadences. Those later checks evaluated individual cycles under additional onset and offset requirements; their denominator differs from the original twelve channel-mean checks. The improvement did not transfer directly to the live mechanical loop: coupled trials either reached the predictive knee guard or completed without satisfying the retained rhythm and PF-timing requirements. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_pf_timing} distinguishes the original failure, offline timing success, transmitted live behavior, and unsuccessful physical acceptance. Together these results show why an output fit and a favorable neural replay require separate checks before promotion to a coupled experiment.

In the original syn6 evaluation, none of twelve channels passed the combined timing criteria. Three components per side explained \qty{99}{\percent} of the centered variance in transmitted PF activity, compared with six components for the intended primitives. One channel remained active throughout the cycle. The corresponding s3k signals required two components per side, but that design lacked quantitative target windows against which to score individual channels.\par}

A reduced Rybak implementation distinguishes a missing motor burst with preserved RG phase from a resetting perturbation, and reduced Deng-derived tests separate RG, PF, and MN stimulation \citep{rybak_modelling_2006,deng_neuromechanical_2019}. Their protocols and limitations remain in Appendix~\ref{sec:rybak_verification} and Appendix~\ref{sec:app_layer_stimulus}. They test specified circuit mechanisms rather than biological validity of the full robot controller.
rows.revised_exact:
{\interlinepenalty=10000 Adjusting synaptic gains alone improved the syn6 fit without bringing any of its twelve channels within the timing criteria. RG-triggered relays and native SNS timing circuits addressed the timing directly. At nominal cadence the native circuit passed all 48 channel-cycle checks. Adaptive timing passed at six prescribed replay cadences. These checks scored individual cycles, including onset and offset, whereas the original twelve checks scored channel means. When live sensory input replaced prescribed replay, coupled trials reached the predictive knee limit or finished without meeting the rhythm and PF timing criteria. The next design question is how sensory input shifts the onset and termination of PF transmission. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_pf_timing} gives the replay and coupled-body tests.\par}

rows.original_exact: The newer 108-neuron, 216-connection W2L model supplies a separate supported-ground example. A bounded calibration produced eight left and seven right qualifying unloaded, whole-foot-clear swings in \qty{10}{\second}, with all qualified transitions alternating. Minimum anatomical knee flexion over $1\leq t<10$\,s was \ang{2.087} on the right and \ang{1.946} on the left. The selected trajectory repeated byte-exactly in a fresh process.
